title: Email Finder Cost: What One Verified Email Really Costs
desc: We priced Apollo, Hunter, Snov.io, Anymail Finder and RocketReach on the only number that matters: the cost of one verified, usable email address. Vendor figures, our arithmetic.
keywords: email finder cost, cost per verified email, email finder pricing, apollo credits cost, hunter credits, snov credits, anymail finder pricing, rocketreach exports, cost per lead email
body:
Short answer. On annual billing, at a steady 5,000 addresses a month, one verified email address costs about 1.5 cents on Snov.io, 2.0 cents on Anymail Finder, 2.1 cents on Hunter. Apollo, the tool we earn a commission on, cannot be bought at that volume for less than 7.1 cents an address. RocketReach could not be priced this way: its annual plans meter exports rather than addresses, and its monthly prices did not render in our session, so we are not publishing them. Those four numbers are not what any of the pricing pages advertise, and the gap is the point of this guide.

All of these tools price themselves in credits, and a credit is not an email address. Two things turn one into the other: the charge trigger, which decides whether you pay for the attempt or the result, and the unit, which decides whether a verification, an export or a second seat costs you again. Get those wrong and your real cost per usable address can be several times the headline.

Every figure below was read on 21 September 2026 off each vendor's own pricing page, help centre or developer docs. Where a vendor publishes arithmetic, we checked it. Where a number is not published, we say so rather than guess.

What one credit costs on each tool

All figures are annual billing, the cheapest published route, one seat.

  • Hunter: 1.70 cents on Starter (408 dollars a year, 24,000 credits), 1.04 on Growth, 0.84 on Scale (2,508 for 300,000).
  • Snov.io: 2.93 cents on Starter (29.25 a month, 1,000 credits), 1.49 on Pro S, 0.71 on Pro M (141.75 for 20,000).
  • Apollo: 1.96 cents on Basic (49 per seat per month, 30,000 credits a year), 1.98 on Professional, 1.98 on Organization.
  • Anymail Finder: published on its own page, from 4.8 cents at the smallest yearly tier down to 0.5 cents at 1.2 million credits.
  • RocketReach: no per-credit price is published. Annual plans meter exports instead.

Two things those rates miss, both in the buyer's favour and neither available on Apollo. Hunter's Bulk Domain Search is 1 credit for up to 10 emails and Anymail Finder's company search is 1 credit for up to 20 verified emails, so domain style prospecting costs a fraction of the figures below. And Anymail Finder sells one off credit packs valid 12 months: 100,000 for 1,090 dollars is 1.82 cents, beating its own 60,000 subscription at the volume we test below.

Now the part the tables leave out: those credits buy different things.

A credit is not an address

On Hunter, the credit table in its help centre charges 1 credit per email found and a further 0.5 credit per verification. So one found and verified address is 1.5 credits, not one. On Anymail Finder, verification is bundled: its own page says you are "never charged extra to verify a found email", so its published price per credit really is its price per verified address. On Snov.io, the pricing FAQ prices a prospect found and an email verified at 1 credit each, while its help centre says prospecting tools do not charge for invalid results, duplicates or empty searches. We read a found, valid, new prospect as one credit. Snov.io does not state that total anywhere, so treat it as our reading. On Apollo, its pricing FAQ says accessing a contact's email uses 1 credit, and a phone number uses 8. It publishes no verification step and no verification price, so the Apollo figures here are the cost of getting an address, not of proving it deliverable. Every other cost per address in this guide has a verification in it, charged or bundled.

On RocketReach, there is no address unit at all. Its knowledge base draws the line plainly: "A lookup pulls contact data into RocketReach. An export takes it out." On annual plans lookups are unlimited and exports are capped: 1,200 a year on Essentials, 3,600 on Pro, 20,000 on Ultimate, or 27.4, 23.0 and 8.5 cents per contact taken out. Essentials is email only; Pro and Ultimate also bundle verified mobile and direct phones, which no other price here does. RocketReach prints the export cap on the same card as the word unlimited, so this is a mismatch of units rather than anything hidden, but a buyer comparing it to a per-credit price is comparing two different products.

The same volume on every tool

A per-credit rate is a step function, not a rate: you only get the good one if your volume lands on a tier. So here is the like-for-like test. 5,000 verified addresses a month, 60,000 a year, annual billing, smallest plan that actually fits.

  • Snov.io Pro S, 5,000 credits a month, 891 dollars a year: 1.49 cents an address, an exact fit with nothing wasted.
  • Anymail Finder, 60,000 credits a year, 1,188 dollars: 1.98 cents, also an exact fit.
  • Hunter Growth, 120,000 credits a year, 1,248 dollars: 2.08 cents. This volume needs 90,000 credits and Starter holds 24,000, so a quarter of Growth goes unused.
  • Apollo: not cleanly computable, and the honest range runs against us. Professional's 48,000 credits per seat is short of the 60,000 this volume needs. Organization clears it at 72,000, but Apollo's own card prices it at 119 dollars per seat with a three seat minimum, so the smallest purchase is 4,284 dollars for 216,000 credits: 7.14 cents an address, most of it capacity you did not ask for. Mixing in a cheaper seat might beat that, but Apollo grants credits per seat and we could not verify whether they pool, so we are not publishing that figure.
  • RocketReach: not computable. Its largest self-serve annual plan exports 20,000 contacts a year, a third of this volume. Custom team plans start at 6,000 dollars a year and publish no export cap.

Apollo is the tool we earn a commission on, and at this volume it is the most expensive here by a wide margin. That is the honest result. The usual defence is that Apollo buys more than addresses, and it does: a US dialler, warmup, website visitor identification. But its own knowledge base lists all three among the twelve things that draw on credits, so one seat cannot deliver 72,000 addresses and a calling programme. Snov.io's 891 adds 25,000 campaign recipients and unlimited seats. Anymail Finder's 1,188 buys addresses and nothing else. A cost per address table compares meters, not value, and the cheapest meter is usually the narrowest product.

If you want the platform, Apollo is free to start, so watch your own credit burn before committing to a tier. If all you need is addresses, a single purpose finder costs less per address.

Who charges you for a miss

This is where the money leaks, and most of these vendors are fair about it. Hunter's help centre says "no credits are used if Hunter can't find or verify an email". RocketReach says "a lookup is used if we find and verify email or phone, otherwise it is refunded". Anymail Finder says "if a search doesn't return a verified email, it's free". Snov.io's prospecting rule is the broadest: in its prospecting tools "you will not be charged credits for prospects with invalid emails (marked as Invalid), for contacts you already saved before, or searches with no emails found". Apollo's developer docs describe people enrichment as "charged only if credit-consuming data is found".

Two exceptions are worth knowing before you budget. Anymail Finder's standalone verifier, used on addresses you got somewhere else, is 0.2 credits "charged for every check", result or no result. And Apollo's waterfall enrichment, the feature that reaches out to other data vendors when Apollo's own record is thin, can flip the meter: Apollo's own documentation warns that "some vendors consume credits per lookup even when no data is found", and puts email waterfall at "typically 1-4 credits" with some configurations reaching "20+ credits". On Professional that is roughly 2 cents at best and 40 cents or more at worst for the same single address. Test a waterfall configuration on ten records before you run it on ten thousand.

Snov.io bills an invalid email two ways

Here is the oddest thing we found, and it is documented on two of Snov.io's own help pages. Through a prospecting tool, an email that comes back invalid costs you nothing. Through the standalone Email Verifier, "each email checked costs 1 credit when the result is valid (green) or invalid (red)", and only an unverifiable yellow result is free. Same vendor, same outcome, opposite bills, decided entirely by which door you came in through. If you are cleaning a list you already own, that door costs you full price on every dud.

Apollo has no volume discount on data

Divide each Apollo tier's annual price by its published credit allowance and you get 1.960 cents on Basic, 1.975 on Professional and 1.983 on Organization. The price per credit is flat within about one percent from bottom to top, and it actually rises slightly. Every other tool here discounts hard with volume: Hunter falls by half from Starter to Scale, Snov.io by a factor of four, Anymail Finder by nine.

The practical consequence is simple. On Apollo you upgrade for features, seats and limits, never for cheaper data. On the others, upgrading is itself the cost lever. Worth saying plainly since Apollo is our affiliate: on data price alone, moving up Apollo's ladder buys you nothing.

How to price your own list

The number none of these vendors can give you is your own hit rate, and it moves your cost more than any tier does. Every coverage and accuracy figure on these pricing pages is the vendor's own measurement, including Anymail Finder's 97 percent delivery guarantee and Snov.io's roughly 2 percent bounce rate. Treat them as claims to test, not facts. So test them. Take 200 real rows from your actual target list, run them through two tools on free or entry plans, and divide what you were charged by the number of addresses that survived a send. No free tier here is big enough for a 200 row test inside one month: Apollo's free plan grants 900 credits a year but releases them monthly, Hunter's gives 50 a month, and Anymail Finder's free allowance is a 100 credit trial that asks for a card. Budget an entry tier for the test, or run it across two months. That is your cost per verified email, and it is the only version of the number that is about your market rather than ours. Deliverability then decides whether those addresses are worth anything, which is a separate budget line and the subject of our guide to cold email infrastructure. If you would rather skip the tooling question entirely and receive a list that is already verified, that is what our lead generation service does.

The bottom line

Ask a vendor three questions before you look at the price. What does one credit actually buy, one address or one attempt? Does a verification cost extra? And is there a second meter, an export cap or a seat minimum, between the credit and the address in your sending tool? Answer those and the cheapest plan on the page is usually not the cheapest address in your inbox.

For a pure address budget, Anymail Finder is the cheapest per credit at the top end, 0.8 cents from 300,000 a year, and Snov.io Pro M at 0.71 cents is the cheapest plan a normal team would actually buy. If the addresses feed sequences, calls and a pipeline you would otherwise buy separately, start on Apollo's free plan and upgrade only when the credit ceiling bites. Whichever you pick, price it per verified address rather than per credit, and re-run the sum on your first real list.
faqs: What is a realistic cost per verified email in 2026?

On annual billing at around 5,000 addresses a month, our arithmetic on published vendor figures puts it between 1.5 and 2.4 cents on Snov.io, Anymail Finder, Hunter and Apollo. Very small volumes cost far more: the entry tiers run from 1.96 cents on Apollo Basic and about 2.9 cents on Snov.io Starter up to 4.8 cents on Anymail Finder's smallest yearly plan. Your own hit rate can move the real figure well outside that range.
Does a failed email search cost a credit?

Usually not. Hunter, RocketReach, Anymail Finder, Snov.io and Apollo all state in their own documentation that a search returning nothing is free or refunded. The two exceptions we found are Anymail Finder's standalone verifier, which charges 0.2 credits for every check whatever the result, unless you re-run the same check inside 30 days, and Apollo's waterfall enrichment, where Apollo warns that some third party vendors in your configuration charge per lookup even when no data comes back.
Is Apollo expensive compared to a dedicated email finder?

Per address, yes. Apollo works out at about 1.96 to 1.98 cents per credit on every paid tier, and one credit reveals one email. Snov.io Pro M is 0.71 cents per address at high volume and Hunter Scale is 0.84 cents per credit, which is 1.25 cents per found and verified address. Apollo's plans include sequences, a US dialler, warmup and deal management, so the fair comparison is against a whole stack rather than against a lookup tool. Note that those features draw on the same credits. We earn a commission if you start an Apollo plan, which is why we are publishing the number that goes against us.
Why does Hunter cost 1.5 credits per address rather than 1?

Hunter's published credit table charges 1 credit for an email found and 0.5 credit for a verification, so a found and verified address is 1.5 credits. On paid plans Hunter then re-verifies that lead every month at no extra cost, but the first verification is still charged.
What is the catch with RocketReach's unlimited emails?

Nothing hidden, but the unit is different. On annual plans RocketReach gives unlimited lookups inside the app and caps exports, at 1,200 a year on Essentials, 3,600 on Pro and 20,000 on Ultimate. An export is what moves a contact into your CRM, your CSV or your sending tool. That works out at 27.4, 23.0 and 8.5 cents per exported contact, and the cap is printed on the same card as the word unlimited.
Should I buy the biggest plan to get the cheapest emails?

On Hunter, Snov.io and Anymail Finder, yes, volume cuts the per credit price sharply, but only if your usage lands on a tier, because unused credits are usually waste, though Anymail Finder says its own roll over with no cap while the subscription is active. On Apollo it makes no difference: its price per credit is flat within about one percent across Basic, Professional and Organization, so you upgrade Apollo for features and seats rather than for cheaper data.
